issues: The correction calls the 'right to privacy' a '19th-century coinage', but no source supports that. Whether the phrase was 'coined' then cannot be verified; 'right of privacy' appears in earlier 19th-century easement law and a first use cannot be pinned down. What can be sourced is that the legal right was first proposed by Warren and Brandeis in 1890. The Constitution Annotated says: 'This right was first proposed by Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis in an 1890 Harvard Law Review article' (FOUND). The sentence is reworded and the source added.

'English courts in 1604 held' should be singular: Semayne's Case was one decision of the King's Bench. Coke reported it as Attorney General and was not the judge, even though the OLL page's framing calls him 'The English judge'.

The source[0] note dates the Oath to the 'late 5th or 4th century BCE'. That range is too narrow: scholarly dates run from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE. The note is aligned with the concepts-1 verdict on the Hippocratic Oath record.
Checked and correct: both quotes, the verdict MISLEADING, and 'limiting even the sheriff's entry'. OLL: 'strict limits on how Sheriffs may enter a person’s house'.

fieldFixes.correction: The right to privacy was first proposed as a distinct legal right in 1890, by Warren and Brandeis, but the expectations behind it are far older: the Hippocratic Oath binds the physician to keep secret what he sees and hears in patients' lives, and an English court in 1604 (Semayne's Case) held that a man's house is his 'Castle and Fortress', limiting even the sheriff's entry.

The page does not name the translator. Dating: the Greek text is placed anywhere from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE, so any single date is approximate.

issues: The correction overstates the Census judgment. It says people who fear being recorded 'stop exercising their rights'. The court's wording is hedged: people who expect that attending an assembly or a citizens' initiative will be recorded 'might decide to forgo the exercise of their respective fundamental rights (Arts. 8 and 9 of the Basic Law)'. The quoted source[0] sentence is about avoiding 'non-conformist behaviour', not about exercising rights. The correction is reworded and source[0]'s quote replaced with the sentence that supports it (FOUND).

The claim that Solove counts 'shifts of power' as a harm was not covered by the quoted Solove sentence. The same passage covers it: 'a particular activity can upset the balance of social or institutional power in undesirable ways' (FOUND). The source[1] quote is widened.

Church Committee: the quote comes from the staff report 'COINTELPRO: The FBI's Covert Action Programs Against American Citizens' in Book III, which is formally 'Supplementary Detailed Staff Reports on Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans'. The cover date is 'APRIL 23 (under authority of the order of APRIL 14), 1976', so the record's date is correct. The title is made more precise. 'The Church Committee found' is acceptable because the staff reports are part of the committee's final report.

fieldFixes.correction: Privacy harms are not limited to exposing wrongdoing. Germany's Constitutional Court held in 1983 that people who expect their attendance at an assembly or citizens' initiative to be recorded may give up exercising those rights; Solove's taxonomy counts chilled behaviour and shifts in the balance of power as harms; and the Church Committee found the FBI's COINTELPRO went 'far beyond' anyone involved in violence.

sourceFixes.quote: If individuals anticipate that participation in an assembly or a citizens’ initiative, for instance, was going to be recorded by the authorities and could thus expose them to certain risks, they might decide to forgo the exercise of their respective fundamental rights (Arts. 8 and 9 of the Basic Law).
